A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MA-RLHF work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–G support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original Gemma/CodeGemma experiments, reward-model scores, GPT-4 and human evaluations, APPS pass@k results, and ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds baseline comparisons, Llama-3.2-3B results, termination-strategy experiments, and human-annotator agreement statistics.

M1.justification: Appendix D.2 adds a code-specific adaptation of parsing-based termination using a programming-language parser for APPS; v1 describes natural-language constituency parsing. The core MA-PPO update, value aggregation, GAE procedure, and Appendix E implementation remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate summarization on TL;DR, dialogue on HH-RLHF, question answering on WebGPT Comparisons, and Python generation on APPS. The added experiments reuse these tasks and datasets. Llama-3.2-3B expands model configurations, while mathematical reasoning remains future work.

E2.justification: v2 Appendix C.3 actually evaluates DPO on TL;DR and HH-RLHF and RLOO on TL;DR against PPO and MA-PPO using Gemma-2B (Table 7 and Figure 17). These methods were discussed or cited in v1 but not evaluated as those baselines, substantially broadening the alignment-method comparisons.

E3.justification: The added experiments introduce DPO-specific learning rates and beta values, RLOO sampling with K=4, and a Llama-3.2-3B configuration with actor/critic learning rates of 5e-6/1e-5 and KL coefficient 0.1. Existing data splits, evaluation metrics, sample sizes, and Table 5 settings are retained; the PDFs do not establish revisions to the original runs.

E4.justification: v2 adds cross-family validation on Llama-3.2-3B (C.4), extends comparisons of termination strategies to dialogue and code generation (D.2), and adds direct MA-PPO-versus-PPO reward-distribution analyses (D.3). Together these substantially broaden supplementary validation beyond the retained action-length, value-estimation, temperature, and rejection-sampling studies.

E5.justification: Appendix F.2 newly reports inter-rater agreement: 64% for TL;DR, 72% for HH-RLHF, and 68% overall across 100 samples. The three-annotator arrangement and 50 samples per task were already documented. Existing standard-deviation reporting is retained, without newly specified training seeds or run counts.

E6.justification: Original Tables 1–3 retain their results, but substantial additional outcomes appear. Table 7 reports TL;DR RM scores of 0.03 for DPO, 0.81 for RLOO, and 1.40 for MA-PPO; Table 8 reports Llama PPO/MA-PPO scores of 3.33/3.96. The APPS table body in Table 10 adds overall pass@1 of 5.56 for parsing versus 5.45 for fixed 10-grams. New GPT-4 comparisons and annotator-agreement results also appear.

T1.justification: Section 2.2 corrects the reshaped reward from adding KL(SFT || policy) to subtracting KL(policy || SFT), and explicitly includes the prompt in the state definition. Section 3.2.1 corrects token indices and the monotonicity interval in perplexity-based termination. These are limited formal corrections; no new theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The introduction and conclusion refine the claim of 1.7–2 times faster convergence into faster learning or reaching vanilla-RLHF reward parity sooner. The principal macro-action contribution, claimed task improvements, and scalability claims remain intact.

C2.justification: v2 explains the computational constraint motivating retention of the pretrained vocabulary/action space and adds mathematical and complex reasoning to future applicability questions. It interprets the new experiments as supporting generalization across model families and benefits from linguistic parsing. Existing rule-based termination, scaling, and WebGPT reward-hacking limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 changes the promised code/data release to stated availability and adds a reproducibility statement covering checkpoints and supplementary training/evaluation code. It also documents new baseline and Llama hyperparameters, identifies RedBaron for code parsing, specifies histogram checkpoints, and elaborates human annotation instructions. Original implementation listings and training settings remain.

R1.justification: v2 adds GRPO to the sequence-level connection in Section 3.2.3, incorporates work such as Shao et al. (2024) and Sun et al. (2025), updates REINFORCE attribution, and removes Bengio et al. (2013). These are limited positioning and citation updates within the retained macro-action and credit-assignment framing.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and appendix organization are preserved. Changes include localized rewriting of preliminaries, method explanations and limitations, terminology edits, new appendix subsections, a reproducibility statement, acknowledgments, and the ICLR 2025 publication header. There is no extensive narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 7–10 and Figure 17, expands the former Figure 19 into four panels, redraws Figure 1, and revises plot annotations, captions, sizing, and placement. Most existing displays retain their content and format. The newly added Tables 9 and 10 have their dataset/metric captions swapped.

improvement.justification: The additional DPO/RLOO comparisons, Llama validation, and termination analyses strengthen evidence beyond v1's PPO- and Gemma-focused evaluation. Formal corrections, annotation agreement, and reproducibility details also help. These are a limited net improvement: swapped Tables 9–10 captions and insufficient qualification of DPO's mixed HH-RLHF findings—GPT-4 favors DPO over PPO, while RM scores favor PPO—introduce reporting problems without outweighing the benefits.
